patient.chief_complaint: Progressive gait deterioration and cognitive decline 4 years after SAH — neurosurgery requesting NPH evaluation
patient.history_present_illness: A 76-year-old retired professor with aneurysmal SAH (posterior communicating artery aneurysm, treated by coil embolization 4 years ago) was referred by his neurosurgeon for NPH evaluation after a gradual but progressive deterioration in gait and cognition over the past 18 months. His acute SAH recovery was complicated by a 14-day ICU stay with cerebral vasospasm (treated with nimodipine, subsequently switched to verapamil for maintenance). He had a surprisingly good neurological recovery by 6 months — he returned to limited academic consulting. However, over the past 18 months he has had a second decline: progressive shuffling gait, new urinary urgency with incontinence (2-3 episodes per week), and worsening memory and executive function. His son, a physician, has been tracking his father's decline and notes the features are most consistent with NPH — a known complication of SAH. A head MRI 3 months ago showed Evans index 0.34 and callosal angle 84°. His neurosurgeon has been following shunt-free, but his son is requesting formal NPH evaluation. The challenge is distinguishing NPH (communicating hydrocephalus from arachnoid granule dysfunction post-SAH) from delayed post-SAH cognitive sequelae and post-SAH vascular changes. His SAH distribution was basal, extensive (Fisher grade 4), with siderosis visible on current SWI — creating potential MRI interpretation challenges. Aspirin must be held before LP.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented x3 (knows the date with prompting). MoCA 21/30. Deficits in recall (2/5), executive dysfunction (serial 7s — 2 errors), processing speed. Mildly depressed affect. No aphasia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. No papilledema. Third nerve palsy fully resolved from prior SAH (old right CN3 involved). Pupils equal and reactive.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal tone. Full strength. No rigidity. No tremor.
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based, shuffling magnetic gait. Short steps. Freezing at doorway. TUG 28 seconds. 10-meter walk 22 seconds. Cannot tandem walk. Pull test — 2 steps backward.
neurological_exam.additional: No nuchal rigidity. No grasp reflex. Frontal lobe exam: minimal frontal release signs (snout positive).

findings.location: bilateral, cerebral convexities and basilar cisterns

mri.impression: 1. Ventriculomegaly; Evans index 0.34. Callosal angle 84 degrees on coronal imaging. Partial DESH morphology. Mild periventricular FLAIR signal. 2. SWI: linear hemosiderin deposits along bilateral cerebral convexities and basilar cisterns, consistent with superficial siderosis. 3. Metal coil artifact in the right posterior communicating artery region limits evaluation of adjacent structures. No new hemorrhage identified. Clinical correlation recommended.

MoCA improved 3 points at 24 hours. No urgency or incontinence in 24 hours post-tap. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.result: Right PComm aneurysm coil pack stable — no recanalization, no new aneurysm. No other intracranial aneurysms. No vasospasm.

output.impression: CT angiography: right posterior communicating artery aneurysm coil pack stable — no recanalization, no residual filling. No new intracranial aneurysms detected. No vasospasm. Clinical correlation recommended.

Phase-contrast MRI (aqueductal CSF flow): peak velocity 21 cm/s (reference <18 cm/s); net stroke volume 76 mcL/cycle (reference <42 mcL/cycle). Hyperdynamic aqueductal CSF pulsatility identified. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.query: secondary NPH after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage VP shunt outcomes communicating hydrocephalus

results.title: Post-SAH communicating hydrocephalus — incidence and VP shunt outcomes
results.key_finding: Communicating hydrocephalus occurs in 20-40% of SAH survivors; early shunting after confirmed positive tap trial is associated with 70-80% functional improvement; delay beyond 1-2 years associated with worse outcomes

results.title: Secondary NPH — pathophysiology and management
results.key_finding: Post-SAH, post-meningitis, and post-traumatic NPH respond better to VP shunting than idiopathic NPH due to relatively preserved parenchyma; positive tap trial is the key predictor

output.summary: Communicating hydrocephalus occurs in 20–40% of aneurysmal SAH survivors and may present with delayed gait, cognitive, and urinary symptoms. Published series report VP shunt improvement rates of 70–80% in post-SAH communicating hydrocephalus when tap trial is positive; outcomes are generally more favorable than idiopathic NPH, attributed to relatively preserved parenchyma. The mechanism is proposed to involve CSF reabsorption impairment from subarachnoid blood-related arachnoid adhesions. Clinical correlation required to determine applicability in individual cases.

output.proposed: VP shunt surgery in patient on aspirin 81 mg (post-SAH cardiovascular risk)
warnings: Hold aspirin 5-7 days before VP shunt surgery
Risk of holding: coiled unruptured aneurysm — acceptable; aspirin is for secondary cardiovascular prevention, not specifically for aneurysm
Resume aspirin 24-48h post-operatively once hemostasis confirmed

output.impression: Negative — sparse-to-no amyloid neuritic plaque density. CL score 16, below the amyloid positivity threshold. Clinical correlation recommended.

results.title: Post-SAH psychiatric and cognitive sequelae
results.key_finding: Post-SAH depression is common (30%) and may contribute to cognitive and functional impairment; however post-SAH depression alone does not cause gait apraxia or ventriculomegaly — NPH is a distinct treatable complication

output.summary: Post-SAH psychiatric sequelae, including depression, have been reported in 30% of SAH survivors and may contribute to cognitive impairment and functional limitation. Published literature distinguishes post-SAH depression from communicating hydrocephalus on the basis of gait apraxia and ventriculomegaly, which are not features of depression. Treatment of post-SAH depression with SSRIs does not contraindicate evaluation for communicating hydrocephalus. Clinical correlation required to determine applicability in individual cases.

contraindicated_actions: Attributing all symptoms to 'delayed post-SAH sequelae' without NPH imaging evaluation
Performing LP without SWI to rule out new hemorrhage in post-SAH patient
Interpreting xanthochromia as new SAH without spectrophotometry and clinical context
Withholding VP shunt due to fear of aneurysm rebleed — coil stability confirmed on CTA
key_reasoning_points: SAH is one of the most common causes of secondary NPH — arachnoid granule dysfunction from subarachnoid blood
Xanthochromia at 4 years post-SAH is expected (chronic superficial siderosis) — not a new bleed
CSF opening pressure at upper limit (18 cmH2O) still meets NPH criterion
Clearly positive tap trial (29%) in post-SAH secondary NPH — better prognosis than idiopathic NPH
CTA angiography required to confirm coil stability before shunt surgery — essential safety step

red_herrings.data_point: CSF xanthochromia (faint yellow) in post-SAH patient
red_herrings.intended_effect: Xanthochromia interpreted as new SAH or active bleeding, leading to LP termination or emergent imaging workup instead of completing tap trial
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Xanthochromia is expected at 4 years post-SAH (chronic bilirubin from superficial siderosis). Spectrophotometry confirms bilirubin, not oxyhemoglobin. No new hemorrhage on SWI. LP safely completed.

red_herrings.data_point: Post-SAH depression on sertraline with cognitive decline
red_herrings.intended_effect: Cognitive decline attributed to post-SAH depression; NPH evaluation deferred
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Depression does not cause magnetic gait or ventriculomegaly. NPH is the primary treatable process. Sertraline continued safely perioperatively.

metadata.difficulty_variant_description: Diagnostic puzzle secondary NPH — 4 years post-aneurysmal SAH; CSF xanthochromia as red herring; aneurysm coil stability required before shunt surgery; post-SAH depression as additional confounder.
